docs.title: About me
docs.text:
Hi, I'm Nell. I care about how information gets organized and how to make it easier for people and AI systems to find and use it.

Words are also a cornerstone of my life. My interests led to 8+ years of work in technical and digital content (most recently), a BA in English, and an MS in Library and Information Science. Between the BA and the MS I spent several years working in libraries.

This site holds both my technical writing portfolio and in-progress agentic AI projects. I'm also practicing using a docs-as-code workflow.

docs.title: Personal
docs.text: I'm a big reader, fiction writer, and sometimes-yogi. I'm also teaching myself about API documentation for fun.

docs.title: How I build this site
docs.text: I build this site with MkDocs and host it on GitHub Pages. The source files live in a public GitHub repository. Every change goes through a pull request, automated checks, and a preview before it reaches the live site.

docs.title: Toolchain
docs.text: Tool Purpose MkDocs Static site generator that converts Markdown files to HTML GitHub Version control and remote repository hosting GitHub Pages Free static site hosting, deployed with GitHub Actions GitHub Actions Runs the checks on every pull request and deploys the site when a change merges markdownlint Checks Markdown formatting, including heading structure, image alt text, and blank lines lychee Checks that internal and external links work Vale Checks prose against the Google developer documentation style guide and my own rules pr-preview-action Publishes a rendered preview of each pull request VS Code Local file editing Claude Code AI pair-writing assistant used inside VS Code for drafting and revising content, and for building/testing the AI skills documented elsewhere on this site Terminal Running MkDocs commands and Git operations

docs.title: Workflow
docs.text:
1. Create a branch and edit .md files locally in VS Code, using Claude Code for editing assistance and content review.
  2. Preview the changes locally with mkdocs serve.
  3. Commit the changes and push the branch to GitHub.
  4. Open a pull request into main. Continuous integration (CI) starts automatically.
  5. CI runs five jobs: a strict MkDocs build, markdownlint, a link check, Vale prose linting, and a preview deployment.
  6. Open the preview link that a bot posts on the pull request, and read the rendered pages.
  7. Merge when the checks pass. The deploy workflow publishes the site to GitHub Pages and removes the preview.

docs.title: Deployment
docs.text:
I first deployed with mkdocs gh-deploy from the command line. I then moved to a GitHub Actions workflow that deploys on every push to main, which removed the manual step.

The workflow builds the site with mkdocs build --strict and publishes it to the gh-pages branch, which GitHub Pages serves. It keeps the pr-preview/ folder, so open previews survive a deploy.

Source: .github/workflows/

docs.title: Case Study: Building and Evaluating Two Claude Code Skills
docs.text:
This is my first completed project to teach myself how to build an agentic AI skill, rubric, and eval harness. It shows that I can write precise specs for an AI, test them against a hand-written answer key, and tell whether a score reflects the model or my own documents.

Source and full write-up: github.com/nellcgram/docs-assistant

docs.title: What I built
docs.text:
Two Claude Code skills for documentation work:

  • release-notes turns git commit messages into user-facing release notes.
  • doc-review reviews a document against a checklist.

I built a full evaluation around release-notes: 20 commits, a hand-written answer key, a graded rubric (a case passes only if it meets every criterion), scripted runs, and a GitHub Action that acted as a test gate, failing a push when quality dropped. The doc-review skill was checked by eye, and is less well-developed because it was used as proof of concept.

docs.title: What I learned
docs.text:
1. My first 0 of 20 was my own documents disagreeing. The rubric required past tense and no internal file names, and the skill never said either. Most of the climb to 19 of 20 was making the spec and the rubric agree, not the model improving.
  2. A passing test gate can be nearly blind. I broke the skill five ways on purpose. Four of the breaks still passed, because the rules both skills read are repeated across files and the model followed those. Duplicated instructions make a prompt robust and its tests insensitive.
  3. How I called the skill changed the score more than most rule edits. The same skill scored 20 of 20 with all commits in one request and 4 of 20 with one call per commit.
  4. The skill is right more often than it is consistent. Across 5 repeats, only 9 of 20 cases passed every time, and my own run summaries turned out wrong until I graded one row per case.

docs.title: Known limits
docs.text: All scores come from the 20 commits I tuned the skill against, so they don't show how it handles new ones. The case study in the repository has the CI screenshots, every other limit, and a link from each number to the file behind it.

docs.title: Case study: character job test
docs.text:
Source: github.com/nellcgram/blind-occupation-reader

This is my earliest project where Claude did the most work (creating agents with few instructions) to teach me the overall structure of system instructions. I’m including it to show my thought process.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: I built this to solve a characterization problem. I wanted to submit all manuscript scenes to Claude, then have Claude figure out what job made the most sense for the character across scenes.

docs.title: Problems
docs.text:
1. I wanted the answer to come from the character’s psychology and behavior, not how he or other characters described him in dialogue, in case he was saying he was a soldier but was actually a spy.
  2. I wanted a solution that allowed me to avoid adding the same scenes to each fresh Claude chat.
  3. I was tired of constant prompt engineering, asking variations on the same questions.
  4. I wanted to learn from Claude what system instructions worked best for this problem.

docs.title: Solutions
docs.text:
I asked Claude to build what it needed, then I rewrote the agent descriptions and prompts and used Claude Code to test results, and rewrote again. Each test I ran resulted in a new log of results and a new occupation considered.

The result is a Claude Code skill with two agents. Five independent readers see only the scene text, guess the job, and quote their evidence. A separate matcher compares the verdict with occupations I had already considered. Each run is logged with the exact text used.

My final problem was that this was not a project others could use because it used my own manuscript. I had Claude write sample scenes and rerun the tests so it made a new log and candidate file.

docs.title: What went wrong
docs.text: While testing, parallel agents re-ran the whole workflow, and one pushed a deletion to an unrelated repository. The agents had shell access they never needed. I limited them to reading files and added a permission prompt before any push.

docs.title: What I did not measure
docs.text:
I did not compare the answers with human readers, test subtle or ambiguous writing (the sample is clear on purpose), or try other models.

The agent design, decisions and other problems I fixed are in the full technical case study in the repository.

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text:
I ultimately decided that this was more work with Claude than it was worth. Testing the agents and skill and adjusting the writing took more time than my original prompt engineering and re-submitting scenes had.

The answer I settled on was to use less Claude in the writing process. I interrogated why I had been using Claude in the first place: to get a general sense of the character’s psychology from “someone else’s” perspective. I decided to write many more scenes, let the writing process determine what occupation seemed to fit best over time (possibly many months of writing and revising), and then take distance from the work before I assessed whether the occupation seemed accurate. This felt like a case of outsourcing my judgment to AI too much.

Disclaimer: Written partially by Claude, partially by Nell; edits by Nell

docs.title: Rubric defect: unverifiable is not pass
docs.text:
Found during Run 1.

The problem: The rubric only has pass and fail, so a criterion nobody can check resolves to pass by default. That means it reports "verified compliant" when the truth is "no contradicting evidence found.

Which criteria are affected: 9 and 10. Both need the book text; review sites don't carry heat level or precise content-warning detail.

Why it matters: A rubric that can't say "unknown" will report clean runs forever and stop being useful.

How I'd close it: I want all criterion to be used so I added unverifiable as a permanent third outcome that's counted separately.

docs.title: Grading defect: scoring the corrected output, not the produced output
docs.text:
Found during Run 1.

The problem: Criterion 2 was graded pass because the delivered list already had "The Suite Spot" correctly attributed — the misattribution was caught and swapped before the run was scored. The grade reflected a hand-corrected result, not what the model actually produced.

Which criteria are affected: 2, and any criterion where an error could plausibly be caught and corrected before scoring.

Why it matters: If catching and quietly fixing an error resolves to the same grade as never having had the error, the score stops measuring the model's actual output — the same silent-clean-result problem the unverifiable outcome was meant to prevent.

How I'd close it: Added a rule to the rubric: grade what the model produced, not a corrected version. A caught-and-fixed error is logged separately but still fails that criterion for the run.

docs.title: Grading defect: same-session grading missed a real failure twice
docs.text:
Found when Run 1 was regraded by an independent agent given only the rubric, the exclusion file, and the raw output — no SKILL.md, no prior grading, no case study.

The problem: In Life's Too Short, the main character becomes her niece's guardian mid-book. Criterion 3 exists specifically to catch this, and it was graded pass — twice, across two separate same-session gradings — before an independently run pass caught it. Same-session grading isn't just less reliable in theory; here it produced the same wrong answer on repeat.

Which criteria are affected: Any criterion requiring a careful read of the output against the rules, not just a records check. Criterion 3 is the confirmed case; there's no reason to assume it's the only one a same-session grader is prone to waving through.

Why it matters: A grading process that repeats its own mistake isn't self-correcting just because someone runs it again — it takes a genuinely separate check to surface what it's blind to.

How I'd close it: Regrade with an independent session or agent that never sees SKILL.md, the prior grading, or the case study — not as a one-time fix, but as a standing step for every run. The same pass also surfaced a second, distinct defect (below) that's worth its own entry.

docs.title: Rubric defect: already-read.md criterion didn't specify a pre-run snapshot
docs.text:
Found by the same independent regrade above.

The problem: The skill appends every recommendation to already-read.md right after delivering it, so the file's current state always contains the just-recommended titles. The rubric's wording for "no books or authors from already-read.md" didn't say to grade against the file as it stood before the run — so a grader working from the live file will always see this run's own titles sitting in it and misgrade a passing run as a fail.

Which criteria are affected: 4. Criterion 5 (skip-all-authors) is unaffected — that section isn't auto-appended to.

Why it matters: This isn't a rare edge case; it will misfire on every single future run until it's fixed, because the auto-append behavior it's tripping over is the skill's normal, intended behavior.

How I'd close it: Added wording to rubric.md specifying that criterion 4 grades against already-read.md as it stood before the run started, and explaining why, so a future grader isn't left to guess.

docs.title: Skill defect: instruction and rubric disagreed on what the rule was
docs.text:
Found by the same independent regrade that caught the guardianship failure in Run 1.

The problem: The rubric's criterion 3 already failed a run for a main character becoming a child's guardian mid-book. SKILL.md's own rule never mentioned guardianship — it only said "a child or pregnancy." The regrade worked because the rubric happened to be stricter than the instruction it was supposed to check; nothing forced the two to agree.

Which criteria are affected: 3. No other criterion is currently known to have language SKILL.md doesn't also state, but that hasn't been checked systematically — this one was found by coincidence, not by an audit.

Why it matters: A rubric can only check what an instruction actually says. Here it happened to check for more than the instruction covered, which looks like a rubric strength but is really two documents stating different rules under the same name.

How I'd close it: Added guardianship to SKILL.md's rule directly, so the instruction and the rubric state the same thing. Worth a pass checking whether any other rubric criterion is similarly ahead of, or behind, what SKILL.md actually instructs.

docs.title: Rubric defect: five SKILL.md rules had no criterion
docs.text:
Found on 2026-10-28 by checking every rubric criterion against SKILL.md, the audit the previous entry called for.

The problem: The rubric covered most of SKILL.md, but five rules had no criterion: no main character under 18, high school setting, or YA; a man-and-woman romance; no main character who molests, stalks, or kidnaps (criterion 9 covered only rape, torture, and murder); no value judgments about content; and stating the default genre when no one is there to ask. Run 2's vetting notes show the man-and-woman and kidnapping rules were applied by hand, so the rubric would have scored a run clean that broke them.

Which criteria are affected: None of 1 to 12 changed. Runs 1 and 2 were graded on those 12 only.

Why it matters: A rubric can only fail what it checks. A rule the skill states but the rubric omits is enforced only by whoever happens to notice a violation.

How I closed it: Added criteria 13 to 17 to the rubric. The rubric's murder clause needed no change, because SKILL.md covers it through "no criminal main characters." Rules about adding books to the exclusion file are behavior, not output, so no output-based criterion can check them.

docs.title: Rubric
docs.text:
Until 2026-10-28 the exclusion file was named already-read.md. Runs 1 and 2 were graded under that name, and their records keep it.

Criteria 13 to 17 were added on 2026-10-28 after checking the rubric against SKILL.md. Runs 1 and 2 were graded on criteria 1 to 12 only.

docs.title: Grading outcomes
docs.text:
Each criterion is graded pass, fail, or unverifiable.

  • Pass — positive evidence the criterion is met.
  • Fail — positive evidence the criterion is violated.
  • Unverifiable — the evidence needed to decide is not available from the sources used. Not a pass. Every unverifiable grade must name the entry, the missing evidence, and what would settle it.

Unverifiable is counted separately in results and never folded into the pass count.

If any entry in a criterion is unverifiable, the whole criterion is graded unverifiable.

Grade the output the model actually produced, not a version corrected after the fact. If an error is caught and fixed before the run is delivered, the run is still graded on the error — log the fix separately; it does not raise the grade.

docs.title: Minimum 15 books returned
docs.text:
• Pass: 15+ books, or explanation why fewer
  • Fail: Fewer than 15 with no explanation

docs.title: Books and authors must be real and correctly attributed
docs.text:
• Pass: All books exist, have the correct title and author, and all authors are real
  • Fail: Any book does not exist, has the wrong author, or any author does not exist

docs.title: Main character has no pregnancy or child or guardianship of a child before the epilogue
docs.text:
• Pass: Main characters are not parents or guardians of a child during the book and no main character is pregnant before the epilogue; an epilogue child or pregnancy is optional
  • Fail: A main character has a child, is a guardian of a child, or is pregnant at any point before the epilogue

docs.title: No books or authors from do-not-recommend.md
docs.text:
• Grade against: do-not-recommend.md as it stood immediately before this run started, not the current file. The skill appends every recommendation to do-not-recommend.md after delivering it, so the current file will always contain this run's own titles — that is expected behavior, not a violation. A grader without a saved pre-run snapshot cannot tell the difference and will misgrade this criterion as a fail.
  • Pass: None of the books or authors from do-not-recommend.md (as it stood before the run) appear in the results
  • Fail: Any book or author from do-not-recommend.md (as it stood before the run) appears in the results

docs.title: No books or authors from the "skip all books by these authors" list
docs.text:
• Source of truth: this list is not defined in SKILL.md — it's the "## skip all books by these authors" section of do-not-recommend.md (currently /Users/nellgram/.claude/private-notes/book-recommendations/do-not-recommend.md). Grade against that section, not against SKILL.md.
  • Pass: None of the books or authors from the skip list appear in the results
  • Fail: Any book or author from the skip list appears in the results

docs.title: No author appears twice within one set of results
docs.text:
• Pass: No author appears more than once in the same set of results
  • Fail: Any author appears more than once in the same set of results

docs.title: No novellas
docs.text:
• Pass: Every recommended title is a full-length novel
  • Fail: Any recommended title is a novella

docs.title: No prohibited main-character types
docs.text:
• Pass: No main character is a criminal, mafia member, vampire, demon, alien, or serial killer
  • Fail: Any main character is one of the above

docs.title: Content warnings follow the required format and coverage
docs.text:
• Pass: Every entry with rape, torture, murder, cheating, BDSM, cancer, a main character's dog dying, or a main character with PTSD/other mental illness includes a content-warning line naming it; entries with none of those omit the line entirely; any rape/sexual-assault warning uses the format TYPE (ROLE, TIMING) with TYPE = "rape" or "sexual assault (not rape)", ROLE = "main character" or "secondary character", TIMING = "on page" or "past"; rape, torture, and murder are only present when not committed by a main character
  • Fail: A qualifying content warning is missing, a content-warning line appears with nothing to warn about, a sexual-violence warning doesn't match the required format, or a main character commits rape, torture, or murder
  • Unverifiable: Review-site summaries mention potentially qualifying content but don't confirm whether it occurs, who it happens to, or whether it's on page. Settled by: the book text.

docs.title: Closed-door/open-door heat level noted correctly
docs.text:
• Pass: A closed-door book includes a "Heat level: Closed door." line; an open-door book includes no heat-level line at all
  • Fail: An open-door book includes a heat-level line, or a closed-door book has no heat-level line
  • Unverifiable: No source consulted states whether the book is open or closed door. Settled by: the book text, or a review that explicitly names heat level.

docs.title: Every recommendation includes a link
docs.text:
• Pass: Every book entry includes a link to the title
  • Fail: Any entry has no link

docs.title: Exclusion process kept invisible
docs.text:
• Pass: The response never mentions do-not-recommend.md, the skip-authors list, or why a specific book/author was excluded
  • Fail: The response references the exclusion list, do-not-recommend status, or explains that something was skipped

docs.title: No main character under 18, high school setting, or YA category
docs.text:
• Pass: No main character is under 18, no book is set in high school, and no book is shelved as YA
  • Fail: Any book has a main character under 18, a high school setting, or a YA category

docs.title: The romance is between a man and a woman
docs.text:
• Pass: Every book's central romance is between a man and a woman
  • Fail: Any book's central romance is between two men, two women, or other pairings

docs.title: No main character who rapes, molests, stalks, tortures, or kidnaps another character
docs.text:
• Pass: No main character does any of these to another character
  • Fail: Any main character does one of these. Criterion 9 also fails a main character who commits rape, torture, or murder, so one book can fail both.

docs.title: No value judgments about content
docs.text:
• Pass: No entry or surrounding text judges the content, such as calling it disturbing, problematic, or great
  • Fail: Any entry or the surrounding text includes a value judgment about the content

docs.title: A default genre is stated when there was no one to ask
docs.text:
• Applies only to: runs with no live user turn to ask which genre
  • Pass: The response says it defaulted to contemporary
  • Fail: The run mixed genres or chose one without saying a default was applied
  • Not applicable: a live user answered or named a genre

docs.text:

docs.title: Run 1 — [2026-09-04] (graded against run-01-output.md)
docs.text:
Grading limitation: this run was graded in the same session that produced the output, so the grader had the skill loaded. A grader with only the rubric and the raw output would be more reliable. Noted as a harness limitation, not a result.

Update, [2026-09-10]: Scored against SKILL.md and rubric.md as they stood before the 2026-09-12 edits (guardianship added, the "other books that qualify" note removed, the no-live-user genre fallback added). Differences from the current files are expected, not new defects.

Update, [2026-09-10]: this run was regraded by an independent agent given only the rubric, the exclusion file, and run-01-output.md — no SKILL.md, no prior grading, no case study. That pass caught a real defect this same-session grading missed twice (criterion 3, below) and exposed a wording gap in the rubric's criterion 4 (since fixed in rubric.md) that would otherwise misgrade every future run. Criterion 12 is unchanged but now carries a flagged open question from that pass — see below.

  • Criterion 1 (15 books): pass — 15 entries returned.

  • Criterion 2 (real/attributed): fail — the model's output misattributed "The Suite Spot" to Mia Sosa; it's actually by Trish Doller. Verification (checking all 15 titles/authors, not just the 3-sample minimum, against publisher pages, Goodreads, and reviews) was done by Claude in-session; a manual spot-check of a subset by the grader is what actually caught this one.

  • FAILURE FOUND AND FIXED PRE-DELIVERY, GRADED AS A FAILURE ANYWAY: the draft attributed "The Suite Spot" to Mia Sosa. It is by Trish Doller. Hallucinated attribution — the defect criterion 2 exists to catch. Caught during verification and swapped before the list was delivered, but per the rubric's grade-what-was-produced rule (see rubric.md), this run is still graded on the model's original, uncorrected output. A caught-and-fixed error is not the same as a run that never had the error, and grading the corrected version would have hidden that.

  • Criterion 3 (no pregnancy/child): fail — in Life's Too Short (Abby Jimenez), Vanessa Price, the main character, becomes her infant niece's sole guardian mid-book (her half-sister leaves the baby with her while dealing with addiction), not in an epilogue. Missed in the original grading; caught by an independent regrade and confirmed separately against plot summaries.

  • Criterion 4 (not in already-read.md): pass — none of the 15 titles or authors appear in the specific-books or skip-all-authors sections of already-read.md as it stood before this run.
  • Criterion 5 (not on skip-all-authors list): pass — cross-checked all 15 authors against the skip-all-authors section; no matches.
  • Criterion 6 (no duplicate author): pass — 15 distinct authors.
  • Criterion 7 (no novellas): pass — all 15 are full-length novels.
  • Criterion 8 (no prohibited main-character types): pass — no criminal/mafia/vampire/demon/alien/serial-killer main characters; all contemporary-set.
  • Criterion 9 (content-warning format/coverage): pass, with 2 unresolved low-confidence items with unverifiable (2 of 15 entries)
  • Take the Lead (Alexis Daria): outside sources describe the hero as "sexually harassed," but available reviews don't specify whether this rises to on-page sexual assault or stays verbal/non-physical harassment. The run included no content-warning line for this. If the scene involves physical contact, the entry is missing a sexual assault (not rape) (main character, on page/past) line and this criterion would fail for that entry.
  • The Bodyguard (Katherine Center): one source flagged "suicidal ideation" among the book's content but didn't identify which character it belongs to (Hannah's mother's backstory is the likelier candidate, per other sources' framing of that same backstory). The run omitted a mental-illness warning on the assumption it isn't the main character's. Unconfirmed from primary text.
  • No other entry showed evidence of an uncovered required topic (rape, torture, murder, cheating, BDSM, cancer, MC's dog dying) or a misformatted warning.
  • Criterion 10 (heat level correctness): unverifiable (1 of 15 entries) — The Matchmaker's List (Sonya Lalli): no source found confirmed this as open- or closed-door; the run left off a heat-level line (defaulting to open-door), which is unverified either way.
  • Criterion 11 (every entry has a link): pass — all 15 entries link to a real page for the title (Goodreads for 14; romance.io for The Spanish Love Deception, since no Goodreads URL was confirmed for it during the run).
  • Criterion 12 (exclusion process invisible): pass — the response never mentions already-read.md, the skip-authors list, or why any book/author was excluded. Open question raised by an independent regrade, not yet resolved either way: six entries carry "Note: this author has other books that qualify," and "qualify" implies a pass/fail filter exists, which arguably reveals more than SKILL.md's own format example ("Note: This author has other books on this topic") does. Left as pass pending a decision on whether that wording crosses the line.

Overall: 8 pass, 2 fail, 2 unverifiable (of 12 criteria). Unverifiable = criteria 9 and 10. Both need the book text; review-site summaries can't settle them.

docs.title: Run-02 Output [2026-09-10]
docs.text:
Genre note: the skill's format section says to ask which genre if the user doesn't specify one. This run had no live user turn to ask, so it was not asked — the list below mixes contemporary and fantasy romance (both covered by the skill's README) instead of one genre picked for the user. That's a deviation from a real run and is called out in run-02.md rather than silently matched to Run 1's assumption.

The Ex Hex, Erin Sterling. Genre: Fantasy A witch curses her ex-boyfriend the night he leaves her, and nine years later he's back in town just as everything in his life starts going wrong.

Icebreaker, Hannah Grace. Genre: Contemporary A competitive figure skater is forced to share ice time with the college hockey team's captain, and their rivalry turns into something else.

The Fine Print, Lauren Asher. Genre: Contemporary An amusement-park heir who never shows his face publicly hires a passionate employee to help save the park, and their arrangement gets personal. Content warnings: Main character with PTSD or other mental illness

The Cul-de-Sac War, Melissa Ferguson. Genre: Contemporary An actress who inherits her grandmother's house finds her new neighbor insufferable, and their escalating pranks blur the line between hate and attraction. Heat level: Closed door.

A Lot Like Adiós, Alexis Daria. Genre: Contemporary A freelance graphic designer hires her childhood best friend's gym for a marketing campaign, and old feelings resurface as they work together.

Two Wrongs Make a Right, Chloe Liese. Genre: Contemporary Set up on a disastrous blind date by their meddling friends, a pediatrician and a stationery designer agree to fake-date badly enough to end the matchmaking for good. Content warnings: Main character with PTSD or other mental illness

Not Like the Movies, Kerry Winfrey. Genre: Contemporary

A coffee-shop waitress is horrified when her best friend turns their nonexistent romance with her boss into a hit movie script, forcing her to see him differently.

Heat level: Closed door.

The Dating Plan, Sara Desai. Genre: Contemporary A software engineer and the family friend who once stood her up agree to a fake engagement that benefits them both, and pretend dates start feeling real.

The Spellshop, Sarah Beth Durst. Genre: Fantasy A reclusive librarian flees a burning library with a stash of illegal spellbooks and opens a secret shop on her childhood island home, where a persistent neighbor keeps showing up. Heat level: Closed door.

By the Book, Jasmine Guillory. Genre: Contemporary An overworked editorial assistant is assigned to whip a difficult, demanding author's overdue manuscript into shape, and finds someone unexpectedly sweet underneath.

Funny You Should Ask, Elissa Sussman. Genre: Contemporary A journalist's puff-piece profile of her celebrity crush turns into a whirlwind weekend, and a follow-up interview ten years later reopens everything.

A Novel Love Story, Ashley Poston. Genre: Fantasy A literature professor gets stranded in the small town from her favorite unfinished romance series, frozen in time until she helps resolve its last story.

Just Like Magic, Sarah Hogle. Genre: Fantasy A washed-up influencer accidentally conjures the literal spirit of the holidays into human form and starts using his wish-granting to fix her life. Heat level: Closed door.

The Hookup Plan, Farrah Rochon. Genre: Contemporary A pediatric surgeon looking for a no-strings arrangement ends up hooking up with her high school rival, who's now assessing whether her hospital should be sold.

The Duke Who Didn't, Courtney Milan. Genre: Historical A duke who never told his childhood best friend he owns her entire village returns to finally court her properly, sauce recipes and all.

docs.title: Update - [2026-09-12]
docs.text:
• Scored against SKILL.md as it stood before the 2026-09-12 edits — including before the no-live-user genre fallback was added, which is exactly the gap this run's own genre note describes. Differences from the current SKILL.md are expected, not new defects.

Grading limitations, both carried over from Run 1 and unresolved here: this run was graded in the same session that produced the output, so the grader had the skill loaded (see Future Improvements in the case study). Verification was done via web search against publisher pages, Goodreads, and reader reviews, not by reading the books — the same ceiling Run 1 hit on criteria 9 and 10.

Vetting note: 15 titles were shortlisted, checked against already-read.md, and verified before this list was finalized. 8 candidates that came up during that process were rejected and never reached a draft output: two for violating "no main character who rapes, molests, stalks, tortures, or kidnaps another character" (From Blood and Ash — the male lead kidnaps and cages the female lead, both main characters; Assistant to the Villain — the male lead tortures and kills people on-page as a main character), two for a main character currently having a child before the epilogue (Meet Me at the Lake, Funny Feelings), one for being a sapphic romance (Payback's a Witch — violates the man/woman rule), one attributed to the wrong author entirely on first guess (Meet Cute Club, which turned out to be an m/m romance by different authors, not a Roselle Lim book — caught during verification, before any output existed, so this is a research-stage catch, not a produced-then-corrected error like Run 1's), one for a disqualifying main-character backstory (The Idea of You), and one for a main character sexually coercing a secondary character (Just My Type). None of these 8 reached a draft or final list, so none of it is a case of grading a corrected output — per the rubric's grade-what-was-produced rule, there was nothing here to grade down, since nothing defective was ever produced.

  • Criterion 1 (15 books): pass — 15 entries returned.
  • Criterion 2 (real/attributed): pass — all 15 titles and authors verified via publisher pages, Goodreads, and reviews; all real and correctly attributed. No misattribution reached the delivered list.
  • Criterion 3 (no pregnancy/child): pass — no main character is a parent/guardian or pregnant before the epilogue in any of the 15. This criterion did real work during vetting: it's why Meet Me at the Lake and Funny Feelings were dropped (see above). Given that Run 1's own criterion 3 pass turned out to be wrong on a closer, separate-session look (see run-01.md), this pass should be read as this session's best verification, not as independently confirmed — it hasn't had that same second look yet.
  • Criterion 4 (not in already-read.md): pass — none of the 15 titles or authors appeared in the specific-books or skip-all-authors sections of already-read.md as it stood before this run (per the rubric's since-fixed wording on grading against the pre-run state, not the live file).
  • Criterion 5 (not on skip-all-authors list): pass — cross-checked all 15 authors against the skip-all-authors section; no matches. This list ruled out a large number of otherwise-obvious picks before they became candidates (Ali Hazelwood, Emily Henry, Sarah J. Maas, and others were excluded either by full-author ban or because every title of theirs checked was already in the specific-books list).
  • Criterion 6 (no duplicate author): pass — 15 distinct authors.
  • Criterion 7 (no novellas): pass — all 15 are full-length novels per publisher listings.
  • Criterion 8 (no prohibited main-character types): pass — no criminal/mafia/vampire/demon/alien/serial-killer main characters in the final 15. (Two related but distinct violations were caught and dropped during vetting — see the vetting note above; they involved a main character kidnapping/torturing another character, not a prohibited character type as such.)
  • Criterion 9 (content-warning format/coverage): pass, with 2 unresolved low-confidence items marked unverifiable (2 of 15 entries)
  • Icebreaker (Hannah Grace): multiple sources flag on-page sexual assault as content in this book, but none found specify which character it happens to or whether it involves either main character. No content-warning line was included on the assumption of no confirmation. If it involves a main or secondary character, this entry is missing a sexual-violence warning line and this criterion would fail for that entry.
  • By the Book (Jasmine Guillory): reviewers describe workplace harassment the main character experiences, but sources don't confirm whether it's sexual in nature or general workplace hostility (the one description found says it's "not from the love interest" and reads as non-sexual). No content-warning line was included on that reading.
  • No other entry showed evidence of an uncovered required topic (rape, torture, murder, cheating, BDSM, cancer, MC's dog dying) or a misformatted warning. Two entries — The Fine Print and Two Wrongs Make a Right — do carry a "main character with PTSD or other mental illness" line (past suicidal ideation for the male lead in one, anxiety for a main character in the other), both reasonably well-sourced.
  • Criterion 10 (heat level correctness): unverifiable (2 of 15 entries)
  • The Fine Print (Lauren Asher): sources directly conflict — one rates it 4/5 "explicit open door," another rates it 2/5 with "a few warm scenes." No heat-level line was included (defaulting to open), which is unverified either way.
  • By the Book (Jasmine Guillory): one comparison source calls it lower-heat than the author's other books and "leaning toward closed door," but nothing found states this as directly as it does for the other 14 entries. No heat-level line was included, which is unverified either way.
  • Criterion 11 (every entry has a link): pass — all 15 entries link to a real page for the title (Goodreads for 14; romance.io for Icebreaker, since no Goodreads URL was confirmed for it during this run).
  • Criterion 12 (exclusion process invisible): pass — the delivered list never mentions already-read.md, the skip-authors list, or why any candidate was excluded; the vetting process above is recorded in this grading file, not in the output itself. Same open question as Run 1's: whether a "note: other books that qualify"-style line (not used in this run, since no such notes were added) would cross this line — moot here since none were included.

Overall: 10 pass, 0 fail, 2 unverifiable (of 12 criteria). Unverifiable = criteria 9 and 10. Both need the book text; review-site summaries can't settle them. This run has not yet had the separate- session regrade that found a real, previously missed failure in Run 1 — treat this score with the same caution until it does.

This was deliberately held off when the run was first produced, since appending eval output to a real personal reading-exclusion file without asking felt like the wrong default — done now on request.

docs.title: How to Read Your Explanation of Benefits (EOB)
What Is an EOB?
docs.text: An Explanation of Benefits (EOB) is a document your health insurance company sends after you receive medical care. It is not a bill. It shows what your doctor charged, what your insurance paid, and what you may owe.

docs.title: What This Guide Covers
docs.text: This guide explains each section of your EOB so you know exactly what you are looking at.

docs.title: Your Personal Information
docs.text: At the top of your EOB you will find your name, address, member ID, and insurance group number. Check that this information is correct.

docs.title: The Four Key Numbers
docs.text: Every EOB shows four numbers that explain how your medical costs are shared between you and your insurance company.

docs.title: Billed Amount
docs.text: The total your doctor or provider charged for the service.

docs.title: Allowed Amount
docs.text: The amount your insurance company agrees to pay for the service based on your plan. This is usually less than the billed amount.

docs.title: Insurance Payment
docs.text: The portion of the allowed amount that your insurance paid directly to your provider.

docs.title: Amount You Owe
docs.text: What you must pay after your insurance pays its share. This may include your deductible, copay, or coinsurance.

docs.title: In-Network and Out-of-Network Costs
docs.text:
Your costs depend on whether your provider is in your insurance network.

In-network providers have agreements with your insurance company. Find the "network savings" box on your EOB to see how much you saved by using an in-network provider.

Out-of-network providers do not have agreements with your insurance company. You may owe more than expected. Check the network savings line. If it shows $0, you used an out-of-network provider.

docs.title: Remark Codes
docs.text: Remark codes are short notes from your insurance company. They appear as 2 or 3 letters or numbers and explain details about your costs, such as why a service was partially paid or denied. Find the description of each code at the bottom of your EOB.

docs.title: How to Check for Errors
docs.text:
Errors on EOBs are common. Checking yours can save you money.

  1. Check the date and service. Did you receive this care on this date?
  2. Compare your EOB to your doctor's bill. The amount you owe should match.
  3. Check your network status. Did you see an in-network doctor? Your network savings should not show $0.
  4. Look up any remark codes. The descriptions are at the bottom of your EOB.

If something looks wrong, call your doctor's billing office first. Then call your insurance company if needed.

docs.title: About
docs.text: This sample Help Center article documents a fictional writing application called Scribbler, following documentation patterns used by Google Play.

docs.title: Why I chose this project
docs.text: Rather than document an existing application like Scrivener, the author created a fictionalized interface with similar terminology. The scope focuses specifically on the Story Board view for project outlining rather than comprehensive application coverage. The article emphasizes customization features such as color coding and metadata creation to showcase information organization and discoverability.

docs.title: Content strategy
docs.text:
The article includes information architecture annotations demonstrating a content model designed for single-source publishing within a Content Management System.

The organizational structure follows a Help Center "How to / About" framework that begins with benefits, progresses through tasks and tips, and ends with related resources. Content moves from fundamental to advanced customization options.

docs.title: Writing and design approach
docs.text:
Style standards (based on Google's style guide):

  • Tone: friendly, empathetic, conversational
  • Clarity: 7th grade reading level, active voice, front-loaded sentences
  • Formatting: Sentence case for titles, title case for UI, breadcrumb navigation

Design decisions:

The author differentiated HTML tag usage for both visual hierarchy and accessibility: kbd tags for keyboard shortcuts, code tags for UI elements, and strong tags for conceptual emphasis. Two callout box styles were implemented — blue for informational context and yellow for warnings.

docs.text: Sample release notes were created for a fictional eReader application, drawing inspiration from Google Play's release note style. Reference: Release notes for Google Play Games on PC

docs.title: My approach
docs.text: Rather than presenting technical details, these notes spotlight practical user advantages. The strategy reduces support inquiries while promoting feature adoption.

docs.title: Key elements
docs.text:
• User value first: Focus on what users gain from updates — for instance, "Adds a streak tracker that shows how many days you've read in a row," instead of purely technical descriptions
  • Action-oriented language: Descriptions enable users to understand how to leverage updated features
  • Balanced scope: Mix of major features with performance improvements to establish realistic user expectations
